clue.text: Articulate way of speaking is a plus in post

parts.note: to articulate a thought is to express it
a speaker's delivery is their manner of speaking

explanation.surface: Praise for a postal worker who speaks clearly: good diction counts in their favour on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulate' and 'way of speaking' read as one idea about eloquence, but they are two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedy dispatch is a premium service, an extra benefit offered by the postal system.

clue.text: Parliamentarians were on one side of this chair, swivelling around

definitions.text: Parliamentarians were on one side of this

indicators.note: around tells us the letters of chair and swivelling are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A picture of a Commons chamber where MPs sat on one side of a rotating chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swivelling' looks like the anagram signal but is fodder; 'around' does the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: In the 1640s conflict, Roundhead Parliamentarians fought King Charles I's Royalists, so they formed one side of it.

clue.text: Before ruler, fathers and sons have to meet the standard

indicators.note: Before places the piece for have to ahead of the ruler piece

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, so fathers gives PAS
S is the standard abbreviation for son
must means have to
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword ruler

explanation.surface: Fathers and sons must be up to scratch before they meet the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the ruler first, but 'Before' means the 'have to' piece comes ahead of it, at the end of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass muster is an idiom for being judged acceptable, reaching the required level.

clue.text: Where butt is awfully hot, sat by sunlight

indicators.note: awfully signals that H and the letters of sat are jumbled

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
a ray is a beam of sunlight

explanation.surface: Someone sitting in the sun, their backside getting awfully hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butt' suggests a backside; it is a cigarette end. 'awfully' shuffles H with SAT to make ASHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarette end is stubbed out in a dish kept for smokers' ash.

clue.text: Sacred hearts not breaking any laws

parts.note: H is the card-game abbreviation for hearts
something allowed is permitted, within the law

explanation.surface: Pious hearts that keep every law.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallowed ground is holy, consecrated, so the word is a synonym for sacred.

clue.text: Bachelor poet detailed superficial suffering

parts.note: a bachelor's degree is the first degree a university awards

indicators.note: detailed means cut off at the tail, losing its final letter

parts.note: Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet

explanation.surface: An unmarried poet itemises his shallow woes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' reads as 'thorough' but means de-tailed: BURNS loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The mildest grade of burn damages only the outer skin layer, hence superficial injury.

clue.text: Blunder, as one may in Balmoral?

definitions.meaning: a Balmoral is a laced ankle boot, which one literally steps into

explanation.surface: Royal gaffes at the Scottish castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Balmoral is the royal family's Scottish estate, but here it is a style of boot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to say something embarrassing; literally, to step into footwear.

clue.text: Stock answer about new and current Bullingdon Club members, say

indicators.note: about means the stock and answer pieces go round the other letters

parts.note: Oxo is a British brand of stock cube
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A stock reply concerning new and present members of the notorious Oxford dining club.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bullingdon is an exclusive Oxford University dining society, notorious for its wealthy members.
explanation.definitionFit: Its members are Oxford students, and a student of that university is so called; 'say' marks an example.

clue.text: Problem in pirouettes after a bad feeling

indicators.note: after places the turned piece following A
a dancer's pirouette spins round, so the words before turn back to front

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A ballet dancer's spinning trouble arrives after a pang of unease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pirouettes' looks like part of the dance scene but is the signal that turns 'Problem in' back to front, giving NIMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Animus is hostility or ill will towards someone.

clue.text: After husband leaves, kicks ornaments

indicators.note: leaves means the husband letter departs from the word

parts.note: getting kicks from something means getting thrills

explanation.surface: Once her husband walks out, she gets her kicks from decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ornaments' are musical ones here, not knick-knacks.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, rapid alternations between two notes are decorative flourishes added to a melody.

clue.text: Walk out with host, perhaps Oprah Winfrey once

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of walk and host are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Storming off set alongside the presenter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks an example: her long-running daytime programme ended in 2011, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oprah Winfrey Show was a chat programme where guests were interviewed.

clue.text: The way things stand in lawsuits, ignoring the odds

indicators.note: dropping the odd-placed letters of lawsuits leaves only the even ones

explanation.surface: A view of where matters rest in litigation, whatever the chances.
explanation.definitionFit: Sold in its present condition means exactly in its current state, unchanged.

clue.text: Without cuts in bread, dug in excitedly

indicators.note: excitedly suggests the letters of bread, dug and in bounce about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly tucking into an uncut loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts' suggests slicing the loaf; it means edits to a text.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete edition of a book, with nothing abridged or shortened.

clue.text: Most unusual, smuggling dope in threatened area

indicators.note: smuggling suggests carrying something hidden inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: rarest means most unusual
dope is slang for information

explanation.surface: A strange drug-running operation in an endangered zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' suggests drugs but means inside information.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical jungle is widely endangered by logging and clearing.

clue.text: Train outside of Eastbourne carrying coin

indicators.note: carrying means holding the coin inside the outer letters
the outside of a word is its first and last letters

parts.note: a ducat is an old gold coin

explanation.surface: A train outside a seaside station carrying money.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastbourne is an English seaside town; 'Train' is a verb, not a railway train.
explanation.definitionFit: To teach or school someone, developing their skills.

clue.text: Stop calling drummer loudly

parts.note: Ringo Starr was the Beatles' drummer
FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loudly

explanation.surface: Telling a noisy drummer to quit phoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loudly' hints at sound-alike wordplay, but it is just the music marking FF.
explanation.definitionFit: To end a telephone conversation by hanging up the receiver.

clue.text: Pair of journos about to accept shocking rag's disgrace

indicators.note: to accept means the turned editors hold the jumbled rag inside
about means the doubled editors are turned round
Pair of means the editor piece appears twice

parts.note: ED, an editor, is a journalist

indicators.note: shocking suggests the letters of rag are jolted into disorder

explanation.surface: Two hacks taking on an outrageous tabloid's shame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns the doubled editors into DEDE; 'shocking' jumbles the rag; 'to accept' puts the jumble inside. A rag is a low-grade newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring someone low, humiliating them, is a verb sense of shaming.

clue.text: Chagall's frame on the next page with plant-like design

indicators.note: the frame of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: overleaf means on the other side of the page

explanation.surface: A Chagall painting's frame, shown on the following page with a botanical pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: Marc Chagall was a painter; his frame gives C and L.
explanation.definitionFit: A road junction or motif shaped like the three- or four-lobed trefoil plant.

clue.text: Figure who may inflame aching back

indicators.note: back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: sore means aching

explanation.surface: Someone whose aching back is inflamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' seems to be the aching body part but signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of love stirs up passion; his statue stands in Piccadilly Circus.

clue.text: Reviled old rogue?

indicators.note: rogue as a verb-like signal says the letters go astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A hated old villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rogue' does double duty: it shuffles REVILED with O and, read whole, the clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrongdoer, a rogue whom people would revile.

clue.text: See 5
Person who hates games teacher, last in contest

parts.note: a rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher

indicators.note: last in picks the final letter of contest

explanation.surface: A PE teacher who loathes sport comes last in the competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'games teacher' looks like one unit; 'games' belongs to the definition. In British slang a rabbit is a poor player, especially in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A hopeless performer at sport, who might well loathe playing it, is called this in British slang.

clue.text: Primitive scourge is polished

parts.note: ur- is a prefix meaning original or primitive
a bane is a scourge, a source of ruin

explanation.surface: An uncivilised menace is surprisingly refined.
explanation.definitionFit: Suave and smoothly courteous, sophisticated in manner.

clue.text: Absent-minded copper's distinguishing feature

parts.note: a DI, detective inspector, is a police officer, and the possessive gives DIS
a trait is a distinguishing characteristic

explanation.surface: A police officer's defining quirk is forgetfulness.
explanation.definitionFit: Distracted and inattentive, the French-derived word for preoccupied.
